title: Polls close in Brazil as Lula and Bolsonaro remain neck and neck
description: Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race.After casting his b
body: Polls have closed in Brazil's general election, after voters queued in long lines for a tight first round of the presidential race.After casting his ballot, 80-year-old left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".His challenger, right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".The result is forecast to be close. BBC Brazil's poll aggregator shows that the gap between Lula and Bolsonaro is only two points. If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the election will go to a run-off on 25 October.According to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE), more than 158.7 million Brazilians, including one million people abroad, are eligible to vote in the election.Lula is challenged by 11 candidates, although BBC Brazil's poll aggregator suggests that candidates other than Lula and Bolsonaro will get only about 10% of the vote.The TSE has not set a fixed time for the release of the official results, but they are expected within hours because voting is electronic and in previous elections results have tended to come quickly.A victory for Bolsonaro would extend a wave of wins across Latin America by right-wing candidates aligned with US President Donald Trump, while Lula's re-election would create problems for Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.Some countries, from which Brazilians living overseas are able to vote, have already released preliminary vote count data.In China, Lula won 56.63% of the votes, while Bolsonaro came in second with 31.33%. Lula also won in countries including South Korea, New Zealand and Saudi Arabia.In Israel, however, Bolsonaro won 74.40% of the valid votes. He also won 71.59% of the valid votes in Japan.Today's result will also determine the composition of the Senate from February 2027 onwards, as 54 of the Senate's 81 seats are being contested, representing two-thirds of the chamber.Currently, the largest bloc in the Senate is Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), followed by the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which has served in a coalition government under Lula.In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father, Jair. But the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup and is barred from standing for office.Because of recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has been prohibited from posting on social media or making public statements.Despite these restrictions, there is little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has his father's backing.

schema.headline: Polls close in Brazil as Lula and Bolsonaro remain neck and neck

title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
description: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit. K
body: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people were injured in the latest Russian attack. He earlier said that the Pivnichnyi Bridge's roadway was hit. Kyiv's eight bridges across the wide Dnipro River link the western (right) and eastern (left) parts, and many of the capital's estimated three million residents rely heavily on the metro lines and trains to travel across the city.Some 500,000 vehicles use the bridges every day.The two struck bridges are still standing - but the damage and restrictions to traffic and public transport have caused gridlock in parts of the capital at times."To get from the left bank to the right one and back - it's just hell," Kyiv resident Roman told the BBC on Sunday.Large numbers of commuters cross the river, especially on weekdays. Repair teams are working to fix the damage and officials say they are planning temporary pontoon bridges, ferry services and even a tunnel under the river to keep Kyiv connected.Klitschko also said a separate Russian drone strike had damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenksy said on Sunday morning Russian drones had also attacked a warehouse in the north-eastern region of Sumy, killing one person. Meanwhile, in the central city of Dnipro, six people were injured after a communications facility was struck, he said.Ukraine's Air Force said that overnight Russia had launched 135 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. It said that 125 projectiles had been shot down.Since Merz became chancellor in May 2025, Germany has become the single largest donor to Ukraine. He said the country "needs all our support in the coming weeks", adding: "If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us."Zelensky said there would be "important agreements" made between Ukraine and Germany.The Ukrainian president has made repeated appeals for Western allies to provide more military support to the country, including supplying advanced interceptors that can shoot down new jet-powered Russian drones and also ballistic missiles.The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier this week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.Russian President Vladimir Putin had earlier said his military was carrying out retaliatory attacks following Ukraine's strikes on Moscow's energy facilities, despite the fact that it was the Kremlin that had first launched such attacks.Putin began a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.The Russian foreign ministry on Saturday repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.Responding to the warning, EU ambassador Katarína Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday: "The EU Delegation is staying. Threatening us will not stop Europe's support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters!"German ambassador to Ukraine, Boris Ruge, reacted to Mathernova's post with: "Amen - we're staying".

schema.headline: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit

title: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on SundayByTeklemariam Bekite
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A pro-government soldier standing guard on a street in Ethiopia's Tigray region on SundayByTeklemariam Bekiteditor, BBC Tigrinya, and Jack BurgessRebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF forces have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and federal government forces alongside allied fighters in parts of Ethiopia's northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides. However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

schema.headline: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital

title: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest
description: Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.The claims were made o
body: Three female journalists have accused police officers in India of sexual harassment during street protests in the capital Delhi.The claims were made on Saturday after the force detained scores of young people calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner.In a post on social media, Delhi Police said its New Delhi District had received the complaint, and it had been transferred to its crime branch for a "fair and impartial" inquiry. Thousands of protesters gathered in Delhi and Mumbai cities for a third day on Sunday demanding that Gyanesh Kumar step down over large-scale changes to voter rolls.The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.Videos online show people being physically dragged away from the Jantar Mantar protest site in central Delhi.The accusations by the women journalists include inappropriate touching by some police.Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi said women fear for their safety and the home ministry must "answer for this"."Police dragged me by my hair," Aahna Singh, an activist and student at Jawaharlal Nehru University told Reuters news agency during the protests.She said the police were resorting to "brutality".The Press Club of India has demanded immediate action on the complaints against police officers, saying it was "shocked and dismayed" by the treatment of journalists."Behaviour of this kind cannot be normalised in a democracy. Journalists must be allowed to work freely, without fear, and document those who gather to raise various issues," it said in a statement.The protesters say the voter-roll revision will benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour the BJP during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.The protesters have included supporters of the influential Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) that began as an online satirical movement.The pressure group recorded its first major victory in July when it forced the then Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign after weeks of protests calling for education reforms.The CJP called for the latest protest after a report in The Indian Express, external said that Kumar's two fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.The differences were reported to be mostly over the controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.The Election Commission has defended its way of working and said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process" and that all the decisions were taken unanimously.But the revelations sparked a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation.

schema.headline: Indian police accused of sexual harassment against journalists at protest

title: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says
description: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on
body: US murderer Christa Pike remains critically ill in hospital and her prognosis is still unclear following her failed execution, her lawyer has said on Sunday.Speaking to CNN on Sunday morning, Pike's lawyer Stephen Ferrell said doctors were still trying to clear two doses of pentobarbital from her body.Pike, 50, was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She survived two execution attempts on Wednesday, and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee.Ferrell said: "She's still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill, we really don't know the prognosis yet, and may not know for several days."He didn't believe she had regained consciousness at any point, adding that he has been receiving updates through her medical power of attorney rather than consulting directly with doctors.He has not been in to see her. "She is guarded. I'm not sure who may have seen her," he said.Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong. But Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said he would resign on Saturday."If she recovers - she may not fully recover - and there may be issues about her competence. I mean, we just don't know any of this," Ferrell said. "We have had no discussions about this. The Tennessee attorney general's office so far has not given us any indications of what their intentions will be."He called on the governor to commute her death sentence to a life sentence "at the very least". "She has endured a torturous attempt at executing her," he said. "She's spent over 30 years in prison, most of that in solitary confinement.""We don't know right now - and we may never know - what sort of torture she endured during [her failed execution]."Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer in 1995.She was sentenced to death the following year after a media frenzy around the killing in Knoxville, Tennessee.Slemmer's mother May Martinez travelled to Nashville for the execution, which moved ahead despite last-minute legal challenges. Martinez, who supported Pike's death sentence, told local news outlet WJXX that she "broke down in tears" after finding out it was not successful. "I think that the state owes me a big apology," she said.The state's Department of Correction has defended the use of lethal injections, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins - meant there was a risk she would experience "unnecessary" pain and suffering during a lethal injection.

schema.headline: Christa Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says

title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
description: One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Uni
body: One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by  so-called "vulture funds".The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

schema.headline: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis

title: Ghana bans preaching on buses with jail terms for offenders
description: Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gath
body: Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel. Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both. The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers. Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023."I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves."Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.The new rules have divided opinion. Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board."Get down, I say get down," he shouts.But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world, external, others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent."The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption."We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says."The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income."I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety. Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison. But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message."There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

schema.headline: Ghana bans preaching on buses with jail terms for offenders

title: Why Canada is wargaming a (long shot) US invasion
description: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.Noting the risk was low and the lik
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency."That's just risk management," Carney said.Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims."President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions."I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum."Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared."That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way."It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.So what would it be like if it happened?The first phase of a war could be quite short.According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a weekIts military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt."I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said."They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation."You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

schema.headline: Why Canada is wargaming a (long shot) US invasion

title: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
description: Image source, AFPImage caption, The two candidates leading in the polls are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio BolsonaroByVanessa BuschschlüterLatin
body: Image source, AFPImage caption, The two candidates leading in the polls are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio BolsonaroByVanessa BuschschlüterLatin America online editorUpdated 2 hours agoBrazilians just finished voting in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names. Polls closed at 17:00 Brasília Time (20:00 GMT) on Sunday, with the nation's vast electronic voter system expected to deliver a result within a few hours. The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, is challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro.In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.Here's what you need to know. The man not on the ballotImage source, Nelson ALMEIDA / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, At the launch of his campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro screened a video in which an AI-generated image of his father endorsed his candidacyJair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, has not run for president in this election. Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election. At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.What do the polls say?While 12 candidates are running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro. BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less. If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October. The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out. BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all. Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot. Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.What does Lula stand for?Image source, Olga Fedorova/EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Lula stressed his country's sovereigntyLula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already. He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família. The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.   Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month. There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.  During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky.Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls. What is Bolsonaro promising?Image source, Adriano Machado/ReutersImage caption, Flávio Bolsonaro has been courting his father's supportersFlávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019.The younger Bolsonaro is running for the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) and, while he is widely seen as less confrontational than his father, he is appealing to the followers of the older Bolsonaro by promising to broadly continue in his footsteps. During his time in the Senate, the trained lawyer has advocated a tough-on-crime stance, calling for longer sentences and laxer gun laws, arguing that "decent citizens" should be able to defend themselves from criminals. He has successfully lobbied for the US to declare Brazil-based criminal gangs Comando Vermelho (CV) and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a move that was opposed by Lula. The younger Bolsonaro has also courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry as part of his campaign.He has said that he will cut what he says are unnecessary regulations and "get the state off farmers' backs".Quizzed in an interview with Globo in August on whether he still believed - as he had said in 2019 - that climate change did not exist, he acknowledged that there had been "extreme climate events", but insisted that these events were "cyclical".Flávio Bolsonaro has actively courted Trump and members of his administration by  portraying himself as a loyal ally during a meeting at the White House in May.More recently, he promised to join the US-led anti-crime alliance that the Trump administration has dubbed "Shield of the Americas", should he be elected. What are the main issues worrying voters?Up until a few months ago, Brazilians told pollsters that crime and security were their main concerns.But in the weeks leading up to the election, a scandal involving a jailed banker accused of orchestrating one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases has pushed corruption to the top of the list.The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, is well connected and has ties to many powerful people in Brazil - both on the political right and left.Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).Police have since then opened an investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for suspected corruption and money laundering over the financing of the film.But pollsters say Lula's campaign was also hurt by the Vorcaro scandal, after alleged links emerged between the disgraced banker and an ally of Lula, the Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.Moraes is the man who presided over Jair Bolsonaro's trial and has made a number of subsequent rulings about the conditions of his detention. A police report suggested that Vorcaro had made numerous calls and sent a number of messages to a phone number which officers say is linked to Moraes.The investigators say Vorcaro asked the person with whom he was communicating for help avoiding arrest.Moraes has denied any wrongdoing but these latest revelations mean that, in the crucial weeks before the election, attention shifted away from the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro to those against the Supreme Court justice.Lula has tried to distance himself from Moraes, saying that "no one is above the law", but his rival has already pounced on the allegations against the judge to make political hay. "Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes," Flávio Bolsonaro told his supporters at a rally, using the right's intense dislike of the judge to shore up his own support.

schema.headline: What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro

title: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory
description: Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.S
body: Al-Alimi was unlikely to have made the fierce announcement without the green light from Saudi Arabia, which remains the key backer of his government.Saudi Arabia has been under constant attack as the Houthis try to target the country's economic lifeblood - oil.On Sunday, Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched a ballistic missile and drone attack on Aramco sites in the capital, Riyadh, and the oil-rich Khurais area in the kingdom's east."Both operations successfully achieved their objectives," the spokesman said in a statement. "The strikes were precise, causing large fires at the targeted sites."It is not the first time the group has said it has hit Saudi oil sites. Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on Sunday's claimed attack, but has previously dismissed some claims as misleading, mocking the Houthis for "chasing imaginary victories".But it has once again shown the price Saudi Arabia - and, as a consequence, the global economy - could pay if it launched a new all-out war against the Houthis.In retaliation, Saudi Arabia has also been striking Houthi targets, according to the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel. It said at least two people had been wounded in strikes on Sunday.On Saturday, Yemen's government also said its forces had hit Houthi targets across the country, including in Sanaa, Saada and the group's positions near Taiz in the south-west.

schema.headline: Yemen government announces major operation to retake Houthi territory

title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
description: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to
body: Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel. Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

schema.headline: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
description: For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurrica
body: For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.With just two months left of the defined hurricane season, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all. This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.Strong winds blowing at different speeds and directions at higher altitudes rip apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns.The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes.This year, temperature records have already been broken in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific, with daily sea surface temperatures now exceeding the previous record set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.There have so far been 17 named storms in the basin including nine hurricanes, seven of which were major.In terms of the amount of energy these storms have produced - known as the Accumulated Cyclone Energy - this season is around two and half times more active than normal at this point.El Niño is predicted to continue to strengthen with forecasts suggesting it will reach its peak in November or December.

schema.headline: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?

title: Cornell University president says school 'must do better' after rape allegations
description: Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity hous
body: Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid. Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better"."We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history. "We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said. On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation. At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe. "Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace."As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life"."Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it".New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

schema.headline: Cornell University president says school 'must do better' after rape allegations

title: Rare tornado whips through small Australian town
description: Several people in Ulladulla, New South Wales, filmed the moment a rare tornado came through the town on 3 October.The Australian Bureau of Meteorology
body: Several people in Ulladulla, New South Wales, filmed the moment a rare tornado came through the town on 3 October.The Australian Bureau of Meteorology said the phenomenon was caused by "severe" thunderstorms and that it was "very uncommon to see one in such a populated place". The weather incident caused damage to properties and knocked over some trees, it added.
